passages.title: Moses recalls the failed entry
passages.summary: Moses addresses Israel east of the Jordan. He recalls appointed judges, the scouts’ report, and the refusal to enter Canaan.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how your account of a past decision shapes what others learn from it.

contextNote.title: A speech to the next generation retains the cost of earlier choices
contextNote.text: Moses retells the refusal to enter while addressing people preparing to cross. His own exclusion from the land becomes part of that memory. The account teaches through consequences already experienced by the community. The listeners inherit both a promised destination and warnings from a past they must interpret.

passages.title: Neighboring lands and Sihon
passages.summary: Moses recalls travel near Edom, Moab, and Ammon. Israel must respect those territories. The speech then recounts war against Sihon.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Why must Israel leave some neighboring lands alone?

contextNote.title: The land promise does not give Israel every neighboring territory
contextNote.text: The speech distinguishes Edom, Moab, and Ammon from lands taken through war. Their territories also receive explanations connected with God's gifts. Israel must buy food and water while passing nearby. The account limits expansion in some places even as it describes violent conquest elsewhere.

passages.title: Og, eastern settlements, and Joshua
passages.summary: Moses recalls Og's defeat and the sharing of eastern land. He encourages Joshua before Israel crosses the Jordan.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how receiving a benefit can leave continuing obligations to others.

contextNote.title: Moses must prepare a successor for work he cannot finish
contextNote.text: Moses requests entry into the land but receives a different task. He must strengthen Joshua, who will lead the crossing. Seeing the destination does not become possessing it. His final work serves a future that will continue through another leader.

passages.title: Remember the covenant
passages.summary: Moses urges obedience and warns against images. He recalls Horeb and sets apart three eastern refuge towns.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: What helps you teach God’s commands with care?

contextNote.title: A remembered voice limits what an image can claim
contextNote.text: Moses reminds the people that they heard words without seeing a form. The warning against making images follows that difference in the remembered encounter. Teaching children must preserve what the people actually received. An object cannot simply supply a shape that the account says they never saw.

passages.title: The commandments recalled
passages.summary: Moses repeats the commandments and recalls Israel’s request for him to act as mediator. The Sabbath instruction remembers slavery in Egypt.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how the memory of slavery can shape rest and care for other people.

contextNote.title: The command to rest receives an explanation rooted in slavery
contextNote.text: The Sabbath instruction recalls rescue from Egypt rather than creation alone. Servants must share the rest their employers receive. Memory therefore places a limit on control over another person's work. Compare Exodus 20 to see how the same command receives a different stated reason.

passages.title: Love, teach, and remember
passages.summary: Moses calls Israel to love the Lord and teach these words in daily life. He warns against forgetting after receiving a good land.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies love for God and teaching the next generation. Consider one daily practice that supports remembrance.

contextNote.title: Memory needs daily practice
contextNote.text: These instructions place teaching in ordinary family life. Speech, travel, rest, and work become times to remember. The next verses use the body and home as reminders. The covenant must outlast the people who first heard it. Memory therefore needs repeated acts, not only a single public ceremony.

passages.title: A chosen people and severe commands
passages.summary: The speech commands separation from surrounding worship and the destruction of named peoples. It also recalls God’s covenant with the ancestors.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Read covenant responsibilities beside the harm described in the chapter. Keep ancient commands distinct from present Church conduct.

contextNote.title: Chosen status does not rest on numerical strength
contextNote.text: Moses rejects population size as the reason for God's choice. The speech instead names love and promises to the ancestors. That explanation challenges pride while the same chapter issues severe commands against other peoples. Read the account's claimed gift beside the violence its instructions require.

passages.title: Remember in prosperity
passages.summary: Moses recalls wilderness hunger and manna. He warns that a prosperous people must not claim that its own strength supplied everything.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: The Church lesson asks readers to remember God in comfort as well as hardship. Consider what gratitude changes in your conduct.

contextNote.title: Success can hide the conditions that made it possible
contextNote.text: Moses anticipates people crediting their own strength for their wealth. The reminder of hunger and manna challenges that account of success. Fields, houses, and full meals can make earlier dependence easy to forget. The warning concerns how people explain prosperity, not a rejection of material provision itself.

passages.title: The calf and intercession recalled
passages.summary: Moses denies that Israel receives the land because of its own righteousness. He recalls the golden calf, broken tablets, and his intercession.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how honest memory can resist claims of moral superiority.

contextNote.title: Possessing the land does not prove the people's innocence
contextNote.text: Moses denies that the gift of land follows from Israel's righteousness. He then recalls repeated rebellion, especially the calf. The past supplies evidence against a flattering explanation of their future success. His appeals for mercy also distinguish preserving a people from approving everything they have done.

passages.title: New tablets and care for strangers
passages.summary: Moses recalls replacement tablets and the appointment of Levites. He calls Israel to love God and care for the stranger.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how memory of vulnerability can change your treatment of a newcomer.

contextNote.title: Remembered exclusion becomes a duty toward resident outsiders
contextNote.text: Moses connects care for the stranger with Israel's own life in Egypt. The command follows a description of God giving strangers food and clothing. Love therefore includes material treatment rather than only friendly feeling. A distinct covenant identity still carries duties toward people outside its ancestral households.

passages.title: Teach the words and choose a path
passages.summary: Moses recalls Egypt and the judgment on Dathan and Abiram. He urges daily teaching and names Gerizim and Ebal for future blessings and curses.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider what habits help a family pass on its commitments.

contextNote.title: A description of farming turns the land into a place of dependence
contextNote.text: Moses contrasts Egypt's watering with hills and valleys receiving rain. That contrast prepares the warning about rain failing after unfaithfulness. The land's fertility does not become a resource independent of the covenant. Teaching and farming appear together because daily survival forms part of the speech's argument.

passages.title: The chosen place of worship
passages.summary: The law requires worship at a place God will choose. It distinguishes sacrifices from ordinary meat eaten at home and forbids consuming blood.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how shared worship can shape community life. Keep the text’s unnamed sanctuary distinct from a later identification.

contextNote.title: A central place of worship does not control every meal
contextNote.text: The law distinguishes sacrifices from ordinary meat eaten in local towns. Families can eat that meat without bringing every meal to the chosen place. Blood remains restricted, and support for Levites remains a duty. Central worship therefore changes some uses of food without making all eating identical.

passages.title: Tests of covenant loyalty
passages.summary: The law addresses a prophet, close relative, or town that urges worship of other gods. It prescribes severe punishments.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how to examine a religious claim carefully. Keep this ancient punishment system distinct from present conduct.

contextNote.title: A striking sign does not settle whether a message should be followed
contextNote.text: The warning imagines a prediction succeeding while its speaker urges other worship. The sign's success does not override the covenant's demand. The chapter then extends the test into close family relationships and towns. Its severe penalties show how far this ancient legal account places loyalty above other ties.

passages.title: Food, tithes, and shared provision
passages.summary: The law distinguishes permitted foods and directs the use of tithes. A third-year provision supports Levites, strangers, orphans, and widows.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how your use of resources can include people who lack stable support.

contextNote.title: A tithe can serve people who lack a secure household share
contextNote.text: The third-year provision names Levites, strangers, widows, and children without fathers. These groups receive food within the town rather than relying on a private invitation. The instruction connects sacred obligation with a local means of support. The owner does not keep every benefit of the harvest within the owning household.

passages.title: Release and an open hand
passages.summary: The law provides for debt release and the release of Hebrew slaves. It requires generosity toward people in need and gifts to people released from slavery.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies a willing heart in helping people in need. Consider whether your help preserves their dignity.

contextNote.title: An approaching release must not become an excuse to refuse help
contextNote.text: The law anticipates a lender calculating how soon the debt-release year will arrive. That calculation could leave a poor neighbor without aid. Moses directly challenges this way of protecting the lender's advantage. The command addresses choices before the release, not merely events on its appointed date.

passages.title: Festivals and fair judgment
passages.summary: The law describes Passover, weeks, and booths. It also commands judges to avoid partiality and bribery.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how celebrations and decisions can include people with less influence.

contextNote.title: Festival joy reaches beyond the people who own its resources
contextNote.text: The celebration names servants and vulnerable neighbors beside sons and daughters. A household's produce must support a wider gathering. The reminder of slavery gives this inclusion a reason grounded in shared memory. Joy becomes a practice of making room rather than a reward confined to the prosperous.

passages.title: Judges and limits on kings
passages.summary: The law addresses prohibited worship, difficult cases, and a future king. The king must read the law and limit wealth, horses, and wives.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Which rules stop a king from using his power only for himself?

contextNote.title: The king must live under the law
contextNote.text: The king cannot make wealth, horses, and wives his main goal. He must read the law and avoid pride over others. The rules place royal power under a shared duty. Later king stories can be read against this standard. Success in war does not settle whether a king governs well.

passages.title: Priests and a prophet like Moses
passages.summary: The law supports priests and rejects ways of seeking hidden knowledge. God promises a prophet like Moses. The people must test a prophet’s message.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects the prophet like Moses with Christ.

contextNote.title: A prophet's claim requires attention to what actually happens
contextNote.text: The chapter warns against messages falsely spoken in God's name. It supplies a test involving a predicted event that fails to occur. Religious language alone therefore does not secure the speaker's authority. The promised prophet belongs beside the warning about false claims in this discussion.

passages.title: Refuge, boundaries, and witnesses
passages.summary: The law establishes refuge for accidental killers, protects boundary markers, and requires multiple witnesses. False testimony receives a stated penalty.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider why judgment needs witnesses and attention to circumstances.

contextNote.title: A serious accusation requires more than one person's assertion
contextNote.text: The law refuses to establish a case on one witness alone. It also describes investigation when a witness may be lying. Those protections limit how accusation can become punishment. The surrounding refuge rules also require judgment before acting against someone who caused a death.

passages.title: Rules for warfare
passages.summary: Some men may stay home from battle. Different rules govern attacks on distant cities and nearby nations. Fruit trees receive protection.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Read the restraints and the violence together. Keep ancient war law distinct from present religious duty.

contextNote.title: The rules restrain some destruction while requiring other destruction
contextNote.text: The siege rule protects fruit trees that provide food. Other instructions in the chapter command lethal action against particular peoples. The restraint toward trees does not erase that human cost. Read each distinction rather than claiming the whole chapter describes humane warfare.

passages.title: Unsolved killing and household laws
passages.summary: The law covers unsolved murder, captive wives, and family rights. It also gives rules for a rebellious son and burial.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider whose voice is absent from these laws. Keep the ancient penalties distinct from present family conduct.

contextNote.title: A father's preference cannot remove every inheritance claim
contextNote.text: The law imagines sons of loved and unloved wives in one household. It forbids transferring the firstborn's share merely because the father prefers another wife. That rule limits favoritism without making the household's positions equal. The protection concerns a specific property claim within an unequal family structure.

passages.title: Neighborly care and sexual laws
passages.summary: The law requires help with lost animals and safe roofs. It also gives clothing rules and severe laws about marriage accusations and sexual acts.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: What duties here protect others from harm? The sexual laws reflect ancient rules about marriage and family honor.

contextNote.title: A home's design can create responsibility before anyone falls
contextNote.text: The roof rule requires a protective barrier around a new house. The owner must address a foreseeable danger rather than wait for injury. Nearby instructions also require returning lost property and helping with fallen animals. Care for neighbors includes preventable harm and ordinary practical acts.

passages.title: Assembly, camp, and promises
passages.summary: The law gives rules for the assembly and camp. It protects people who escape slavery. It also covers loans and promises.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider the protection offered to a person escaping slavery. Keep ancient membership restrictions distinct from present human worth.

contextNote.title: An escaped servant receives protection from forced return
contextNote.text: The instruction tells the community not to deliver the servant back to a master. It also permits the person to choose a place to live. This protection appears beside rules that exclude some people from the assembly. The chapter contains different forms of belonging and restriction rather than one uniform policy.

passages.title: Household changes and protection of the poor
passages.summary: The law concerns divorce and remarriage, loans, wages, testimony, and gleaning. It protects certain essential belongings from seizure.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how prompt payment and leaving resources for others can turn compassion into action.

contextNote.title: Daily wages answer a need that cannot wait indefinitely
contextNote.text: The worker depends on payment for immediate life. The employer must pay before sunset rather than use delay as an advantage. Rules about pledges and gleaning likewise limit control over another person's necessities. The remembered experience of slavery gives these economic restraints a stated reason.

passages.title: Fair measures and family continuity
passages.summary: The law limits punishment and requires honest trade. It gives duties toward a dead brother’s family. Israel must remember Amalek’s attack.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider why a fair measure matters when another person cannot verify your claim.

contextNote.title: Small measures can cause real harm
contextNote.text: The rule forbids keeping one weight for buying and another for selling. A hidden difference can move wealth without open violence. Fair measures protect people who cannot inspect every transaction. The passage makes trust a public concern. Its promise of life links daily trade with the community’s future.

passages.title: First produce and covenant declaration
passages.summary: The worshiper brings first produce and recounts the ancestors’ hardship, Egypt, and deliverance. A declaration accompanies the third-year tithe.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how giving can include an honest account of what you received from others.

contextNote.title: Offering crops joins present abundance with a remembered vulnerable past
contextNote.text: The worshiper's declaration begins with an ancestor living without settled security. It continues through oppression, rescue, and arrival before presenting the harvest. The gift therefore carries a story about how food became possible. Sharing with others keeps that memory from becoming only a claim to private success.

passages.title: Instructions for Ebal and Gerizim
passages.summary: Moses commands an altar and written law after Israel enters the land. The tribes must gather on two mountains to hear blessings and curses.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider what a public promise requires when wrongdoing can remain hidden.

contextNote.title: Public responses name wrongs that can remain hidden
contextNote.text: The curses include misleading a blind person and denying vulnerable people justice. The assembled people answer each statement together. Public speech therefore addresses acts that an ordinary witness may miss. The planned ceremony makes shared responsibility audible before the people settle into the land.

passages.title: Blessings and terrible curses
passages.summary: Moses lists blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience. The warnings include disease, defeat, hunger, and exile.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Read the whole warning with care. Avoid using its suffering language to assign blame to someone in distress.

contextNote.title: The warnings describe the loss of an entire way of life
contextNote.text: The curses reach food, health, family, work, safety, and dwelling. Their accumulation makes disaster larger than one defeat in battle. The speech interprets those losses through covenant failure within its own argument. It does not prove that a present sufferer's illness reveals personal guilt.

passages.title: The covenant assembly
passages.summary: Moses addresses leaders, families, and strangers at the covenant gathering. He warns against hidden disloyalty and describes a devastated land.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies inward loyalty and shared covenant identity. Consider the effect of your choices on people who will follow you.

contextNote.title: The assembly includes people beyond its leaders and warriors
contextNote.text: Moses names children, women, and strangers doing basic camp work. The covenant gathering therefore reaches people with unequal positions and duties. The speech also includes future people absent from that day's assembly. Shared obligation extends beyond those who hold the most visible authority.

passages.title: Return and choose life
passages.summary: Moses describes return after scattering and calls the people to love and obey God. He presents the instruction as near and calls them to choose life.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: The Church lesson compares these words with Lehi’s teaching about agency. Consider what choosing life requires in a daily decision.

contextNote.title: Near words still require a choice of action
contextNote.text: Moses says the command is near the people's mouths and hearts. They do not need someone to retrieve it from an unreachable place. That accessibility leads into the call to choose life through obedience. Possessing understandable words does not automatically produce the conduct those words require.

passages.title: Joshua, the written law, and the song
passages.summary: Moses encourages Joshua, gives the written law to priests, and commands public readings. A song will serve as a witness against future unfaithfulness.

contextNote.title: Public reading serves children who did not hear the first instruction
contextNote.text: The scheduled gathering includes people who must learn rather than simply recall. Priests preserve the written law, while leaders make it heard. Joshua's appointment also prepares for life after Moses. Text, public teaching, and shared leadership answer different parts of the same generational change.

passages.title: The Song of Moses
passages.summary: The poem recounts God’s care, Israel’s neglect, judgment, and vindication. Moses then receives instructions to go up Mount Nebo.

contextNote.title: The poem turns nourishment into an image of forgotten dependence
contextNote.text: Israel grows strong through provision and then rejects the giver. The image makes prosperity part of the poem's explanation for neglect. Rock and eagle images describe care in different forms. These comparisons carry the song's argument rather than supplying physical descriptions of God.

passages.title: Blessings for the tribes
passages.summary: Moses blesses the tribes before his departure. The poem names tribal identities and describes their hopes, duties, and regions.

contextNote.title: Tribal differences remain within a shared inheritance of instruction
contextNote.text: The poem names distinct tribes and describes different duties and hopes. The opening still identifies Moses' law as an inheritance for the gathered people. Shared identity therefore does not erase every difference between their futures. The blessings give those differences a place within one closing address.

passages.title: Moses’s departure and Joshua’s leadership
passages.summary: Moses sees the land from Nebo and dies. His burial place is not known. Joshua becomes Israel’s leader.

lds.text: LDS sources teach that Moses was translated. They describe this as a change without ordinary death.

contextNote.title: The end preserves both succession and the loss of Moses
contextNote.text: Joshua receives recognition as the people continue after Moses' death. The closing praise still describes Moses as unmatched in his encounter with God. Succession does not mean the next leader simply replaces every aspect of the earlier one. The unknown grave also prevents the ending from giving readers a fixed burial destination.

events.title: Moses recalls the failed entry
events.summary: Moses addresses Israel east of the Jordan. He recalls appointed judges, the scouts’ report, and the refusal to enter Canaan.
events.detail: Moses retells the refusal to enter while addressing people preparing to cross. His own exclusion from the land becomes part of that memory. The account teaches through consequences already experienced by the community. The listeners inherit both a promised destination and warnings from a past they must interpret.

lds.text: Consider how your account of a past decision shapes what others learn from it.

events.title: Neighboring lands and Sihon
events.summary: Moses recalls travel near Edom, Moab, and Ammon. Israel must respect those territories. The speech then recounts war against Sihon.
events.detail: The speech distinguishes Edom, Moab, and Ammon from lands taken through war. Their territories also receive explanations connected with God's gifts. Israel must buy food and water while passing nearby. The account limits expansion in some places even as it describes violent conquest elsewhere.

events.title: Og, eastern settlements, and Joshua
events.summary: Moses recalls Og's defeat and the sharing of eastern land. He encourages Joshua before Israel crosses the Jordan.
events.detail: Moses requests entry into the land but receives a different task. He must strengthen Joshua, who will lead the crossing. Seeing the destination does not become possessing it. His final work serves a future that will continue through another leader.

events.title: Remember the covenant
events.summary: Moses urges obedience and warns against images. He recalls Horeb and sets apart three eastern refuge towns.
events.detail: Moses reminds the people that they heard words without seeing a form. The warning against making images follows that difference in the remembered encounter. Teaching children must preserve what the people actually received. An object cannot simply supply a shape that the account says they never saw.

events.title: The commandments recalled
events.summary: Moses repeats the commandments and recalls Israel’s request for him to act as mediator. The Sabbath instruction remembers slavery in Egypt.
events.detail: The Sabbath instruction recalls rescue from Egypt rather than creation alone. Servants must share the rest their employers receive. Memory therefore places a limit on control over another person's work. Compare Exodus 20 to see how the same command receives a different stated reason.

events.title: Love, teach, and remember
events.summary: Moses calls Israel to love the Lord and teach these words in daily life. He warns against forgetting after receiving a good land.
events.detail: These instructions place teaching in ordinary family life. Speech, travel, rest, and work become times to remember. The next verses use the body and home as reminders. The covenant must outlast the people who first heard it. Memory therefore needs repeated acts, not only a single public ceremony.

events.title: A chosen people and severe commands
events.summary: The speech commands separation from surrounding worship and the destruction of named peoples. It also recalls God’s covenant with the ancestors.
events.detail: Moses rejects population size as the reason for God's choice. The speech instead names love and promises to the ancestors. That explanation challenges pride while the same chapter issues severe commands against other peoples. Read the account's claimed gift beside the violence its instructions require.

events.title: Remember in prosperity
events.summary: Moses recalls wilderness hunger and manna. He warns that a prosperous people must not claim that its own strength supplied everything.
events.detail: Moses anticipates people crediting their own strength for their wealth. The reminder of hunger and manna challenges that account of success. Fields, houses, and full meals can make earlier dependence easy to forget. The warning concerns how people explain prosperity, not a rejection of material provision itself.

lds.text: The Church lesson asks readers to remember God in comfort as well as hardship. Consider what gratitude changes in your conduct.

events.title: The calf and intercession recalled
events.summary: Moses denies that Israel receives the land because of its own righteousness. He recalls the golden calf, broken tablets, and his intercession.
events.detail: Moses denies that the gift of land follows from Israel's righteousness. He then recalls repeated rebellion, especially the calf. The past supplies evidence against a flattering explanation of their future success. His appeals for mercy also distinguish preserving a people from approving everything they have done.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how honest memory can resist claims of moral superiority.

events.title: New tablets and care for strangers
events.summary: Moses recalls replacement tablets and the appointment of Levites. He calls Israel to love God and care for the stranger.
events.detail: Moses connects care for the stranger with Israel's own life in Egypt. The command follows a description of God giving strangers food and clothing. Love therefore includes material treatment rather than only friendly feeling. A distinct covenant identity still carries duties toward people outside its ancestral households.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how memory of vulnerability can change your treatment of a newcomer.

events.title: Teach the words and choose a path
events.summary: Moses recalls Egypt and the judgment on Dathan and Abiram. He urges daily teaching and names Gerizim and Ebal for future blessings and curses.
events.detail: Moses contrasts Egypt's watering with hills and valleys receiving rain. That contrast prepares the warning about rain failing after unfaithfulness. The land's fertility does not become a resource independent of the covenant. Teaching and farming appear together because daily survival forms part of the speech's argument.

lds.text: Consider what habits help a family pass on its commitments.

events.title: The chosen place of worship
events.summary: The law requires worship at a place God will choose. It distinguishes sacrifices from ordinary meat eaten at home and forbids consuming blood.
events.detail: The law distinguishes sacrifices from ordinary meat eaten in local towns. Families can eat that meat without bringing every meal to the chosen place. Blood remains restricted, and support for Levites remains a duty. Central worship therefore changes some uses of food without making all eating identical.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how shared worship can shape community life. Keep the text’s unnamed sanctuary distinct from a later identification.

events.title: Tests of covenant loyalty
events.summary: The law addresses a prophet, close relative, or town that urges worship of other gods. It prescribes severe punishments.
events.detail: The warning imagines a prediction succeeding while its speaker urges other worship. The sign's success does not override the covenant's demand. The chapter then extends the test into close family relationships and towns. Its severe penalties show how far this ancient legal account places loyalty above other ties.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how to examine a religious claim carefully. Keep this ancient punishment system distinct from present conduct.

events.title: Food, tithes, and shared provision
events.summary: The law distinguishes permitted foods and directs the use of tithes. A third-year provision supports Levites, strangers, orphans, and widows.
events.detail: The third-year provision names Levites, strangers, widows, and children without fathers. These groups receive food within the town rather than relying on a private invitation. The instruction connects sacred obligation with a local means of support. The owner does not keep every benefit of the harvest within the owning household.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how your use of resources can include people who lack stable support.

events.title: Release and an open hand
events.summary: The law provides for debt release and the release of Hebrew slaves. It requires generosity toward people in need and gifts to people released from slavery.
events.detail: The law anticipates a lender calculating how soon the debt-release year will arrive. That calculation could leave a poor neighbor without aid. Moses directly challenges this way of protecting the lender's advantage. The command addresses choices before the release, not merely events on its appointed date.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies a willing heart in helping people in need. Consider whether your help preserves their dignity.

events.title: Festivals and fair judgment
events.summary: The law describes Passover, weeks, and booths. It also commands judges to avoid partiality and bribery.
events.detail: The celebration names servants and vulnerable neighbors beside sons and daughters. A household's produce must support a wider gathering. The reminder of slavery gives this inclusion a reason grounded in shared memory. Joy becomes a practice of making room rather than a reward confined to the prosperous.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how celebrations and decisions can include people with less influence.

events.title: Judges and limits on kings
events.summary: The law addresses prohibited worship, difficult cases, and a future king. The king must read the law and limit wealth, horses, and wives.
events.detail: The king cannot make wealth, horses, and wives his main goal. He must read the law and avoid pride over others. The rules place royal power under a shared duty. Later king stories can be read against this standard. Success in war does not settle whether a king governs well.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

events.title: Priests and a prophet like Moses
events.summary: The law supports priests and rejects ways of seeking hidden knowledge. God promises a prophet like Moses. The people must test a prophet’s message.
events.detail: The chapter warns against messages falsely spoken in God's name. It supplies a test involving a predicted event that fails to occur. Religious language alone therefore does not secure the speaker's authority. The promised prophet belongs beside the warning about false claims in this discussion.

events.title: Refuge, boundaries, and witnesses
events.summary: The law establishes refuge for accidental killers, protects boundary markers, and requires multiple witnesses. False testimony receives a stated penalty.
events.detail: The law refuses to establish a case on one witness alone. It also describes investigation when a witness may be lying. Those protections limit how accusation can become punishment. The surrounding refuge rules also require judgment before acting against someone who caused a death.

lds.text: Consider why judgment needs witnesses and attention to circumstances.

events.title: Rules for warfare
events.summary: Some men may stay home from battle. Different rules govern attacks on distant cities and nearby nations. Fruit trees receive protection.
events.detail: The siege rule protects fruit trees that provide food. Other instructions in the chapter command lethal action against particular peoples. The restraint toward trees does not erase that human cost. Read each distinction rather than claiming the whole chapter describes humane warfare.

events.title: Unsolved killing and household laws
events.summary: The law covers unsolved murder, captive wives, and family rights. It also gives rules for a rebellious son and burial.
events.detail: The law imagines sons of loved and unloved wives in one household. It forbids transferring the firstborn's share merely because the father prefers another wife. That rule limits favoritism without making the household's positions equal. The protection concerns a specific property claim within an unequal family structure.

events.title: Neighborly care and sexual laws
events.summary: The law requires help with lost animals and safe roofs. It also gives clothing rules and severe laws about marriage accusations and sexual acts.
events.detail: The roof rule requires a protective barrier around a new house. The owner must address a foreseeable danger rather than wait for injury. Nearby instructions also require returning lost property and helping with fallen animals. Care for neighbors includes preventable harm and ordinary practical acts.

lds.text: What duties here protect others from harm? The sexual laws reflect ancient rules about marriage and family honor.

events.title: Assembly, camp, and promises
events.summary: The law gives rules for the assembly and camp. It protects people who escape slavery. It also covers loans and promises.
events.detail: The instruction tells the community not to deliver the servant back to a master. It also permits the person to choose a place to live. This protection appears beside rules that exclude some people from the assembly. The chapter contains different forms of belonging and restriction rather than one uniform policy.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider the protection offered to a person escaping slavery. Keep ancient membership restrictions distinct from present human worth.

events.title: Household changes and protection of the poor
events.summary: The law concerns divorce and remarriage, loans, wages, testimony, and gleaning. It protects certain essential belongings from seizure.
events.detail: The worker depends on payment for immediate life. The employer must pay before sunset rather than use delay as an advantage. Rules about pledges and gleaning likewise limit control over another person's necessities. The remembered experience of slavery gives these economic restraints a stated reason.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how prompt payment and leaving resources for others can turn compassion into action.

events.title: Fair measures and family continuity
events.summary: The law limits punishment and requires honest trade. It gives duties toward a dead brother’s family. Israel must remember Amalek’s attack.
events.detail: The rule forbids keeping one weight for buying and another for selling. A hidden difference can move wealth without open violence. Fair measures protect people who cannot inspect every transaction. The passage makes trust a public concern. Its promise of life links daily trade with the community’s future.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider why a fair measure matters when another person cannot verify your claim.

events.title: First produce and covenant declaration
events.summary: The worshiper brings first produce and recounts the ancestors’ hardship, Egypt, and deliverance. A declaration accompanies the third-year tithe.
events.detail: The worshiper's declaration begins with an ancestor living without settled security. It continues through oppression, rescue, and arrival before presenting the harvest. The gift therefore carries a story about how food became possible. Sharing with others keeps that memory from becoming only a claim to private success.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how giving can include an honest account of what you received from others.

events.title: Instructions for Ebal and Gerizim
events.summary: Moses commands an altar and written law after Israel enters the land. The tribes must gather on two mountains to hear blessings and curses.
events.detail: The curses include misleading a blind person and denying vulnerable people justice. The assembled people answer each statement together. Public speech therefore addresses acts that an ordinary witness may miss. The planned ceremony makes shared responsibility audible before the people settle into the land.

lds.text: Consider what a public promise requires when wrongdoing can remain hidden.

events.title: Blessings and terrible curses
events.summary: Moses lists blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience. The warnings include disease, defeat, hunger, and exile.
events.detail: The curses reach food, health, family, work, safety, and dwelling. Their accumulation makes disaster larger than one defeat in battle. The speech interprets those losses through covenant failure within its own argument. It does not prove that a present sufferer's illness reveals personal guilt.

lds.text: Read the whole warning with care. Avoid using its suffering language to assign blame to someone in distress.

events.title: The covenant assembly
events.summary: Moses addresses leaders, families, and strangers at the covenant gathering. He warns against hidden disloyalty and describes a devastated land.
events.detail: Moses names children, women, and strangers doing basic camp work. The covenant gathering therefore reaches people with unequal positions and duties. The speech also includes future people absent from that day's assembly. Shared obligation extends beyond those who hold the most visible authority.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies inward loyalty and shared covenant identity. Consider the effect of your choices on people who will follow you.

events.title: Return and choose life
events.summary: Moses describes return after scattering and calls the people to love and obey God. He presents the instruction as near and calls them to choose life.
events.detail: Moses says the command is near the people's mouths and hearts. They do not need someone to retrieve it from an unreachable place. That accessibility leads into the call to choose life through obedience. Possessing understandable words does not automatically produce the conduct those words require.

guides.title: Deuteronomy: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Memory needs daily practice
steps.text: These instructions place teaching in ordinary family life. Speech, travel, rest, and work become times to remember. The next verses use the body and home as reminders. The covenant must outlast the people who first heard it. Memory therefore needs repeated acts, not only a single public ceremony.

steps.title: The king must live under the law
steps.text: The king cannot make wealth, horses, and wives his main goal. He must read the law and avoid pride over others. The rules place royal power under a shared duty. Later king stories can be read against this standard. Success in war does not settle whether a king governs well.

steps.title: Small measures can cause real harm
steps.text: The rule forbids keeping one weight for buying and another for selling. A hidden difference can move wealth without open violence. Fair measures protect people who cannot inspect every transaction. The passage makes trust a public concern. Its promise of life links daily trade with the community’s future.

textRoutes.title: Moses recalls the failed entry
textRoutes.summary: Moses addresses Israel east of the Jordan. He recalls appointed judges, the scouts’ report, and the refusal to enter Canaan.
textRoutes.detail: Moses retells the refusal to enter while addressing people preparing to cross. His own exclusion from the land becomes part of that memory. The account teaches through consequences already experienced by the community. The listeners inherit both a promised destination and warnings from a past they must interpret.
textRoutes.uncertainty: Moses recalls the Horeb-to-Kadesh journey in Deuteronomy 1. This is a retrospective, simplified line. It omits uncertain camps and does not show an excavated road.
